moduleTitle: SQE1 · Wills and Administration of Estates
title: Family provision claims II: the discretionary factors and adult children
subtitle: How a court weighs a 1975 Act claim on the merits, why independent adult children face an uphill task, and the six-month time limit
objectives: List the s 3 factors a court weighs in deciding a family provision claim, and apply them to a fact pattern
Explain why an independent adult child faces a high threshold in establishing a 1975 Act claim, and the kind of evidence that can overcome it
State the six-month time limit for bringing a claim under the Act and identify when the court may allow a late claim

leadingAuthorities.citation: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 3
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the factors the court must consider in assessing a claim

leadingAuthorities.citation: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 4
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the six-month time limit for bringing a claim, running from the grant of representation
Leading Supreme Court authority on the standard applied to an independent adult child's claim

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Getting an applicant through the s 1 gate, covered in the last lesson, is only step one. This lesson is where most of the real analysis — and most of the marks — actually sit: weighing the s 3 factors, and knowing why the same set of facts can succeed for a maintained partner and fail for an estranged adult child.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the s 3 list. The test pool here is built around applying multiple factors to one fact pattern at once — expect to weigh several pulling in different directions, not spot one obvious answer.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Fix the s 3 factors and the six-month time limit from Parts 1 and 4 before working through the Ilott material — the adult-child discussion assumes you already have the factor list to hand.

overview.hook: Heather Ilott had been estranged from her mother for over twenty years when her mother died leaving her entire estate to animal charities and nothing to Heather. Heather won — eventually — but the Supreme Court's judgment is as notable for what it refused to say as for what it awarded. This lesson is about the discretionary weighing exercise that case exemplifies, and about the one category of claimant — the independent adult child — who has to work hardest to succeed.

parts.heading: The section 3 checklist
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to
body: Once an applicant clears the s 1 eligibility gate covered in the previous lesson, the court turns to s 3, which lists the matters it must have regard to in deciding whether reasonable financial provision has been made, and if not, what order to make. The list is not exhaustive, and no single factor is automatically decisive — the exercise is a genuine weighing of everything relevant.

The core s 3(1) factors are: the financial resources and needs the applicant has or is likely to have in the foreseeable future; the financial resources and needs of any other applicant; the financial resources and needs of any beneficiary of the estate; any obligations and responsibilities the deceased had towards any applicant or beneficiary; the size and nature of the estate; any physical or mental disability of an applicant or beneficiary; and any other matter, including conduct, which the court may consider relevant — this last limb is deliberately open-ended.

Additional, category-specific factors apply on top of this core list depending on who is applying — for example, a spouse's claim also brings in factors mirroring a divorce settlement (age, duration of the marriage, contribution to the family), while a child's claim brings in the manner in which they were being, or might expect to be, educated or trained.

components.label: Core s 3(1) factors
points: Applicant's financial resources and needs, now and foreseeably
Other applicants' financial resources and needs
The deceased's obligations and responsibilities towards any applicant or beneficiary
The size and nature of the estate
Any physical or mental disability of an applicant or beneficiary
Any other matter, including conduct, that the court considers relevant

interaction.prompt: A disabled adult applicant with limited earning capacity applies for provision from a modest estate, against a single beneficiary who is financially comfortable. Analyse which s 3 factors are most obviously engaged.
factsToOrder: The applicant has a physical disability affecting earning capacity
The estate is modest in size
The sole beneficiary is financially comfortable
The applicant's needs are likely to continue into the foreseeable future

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapping each fact to the relevant s 3 factor
Factor list given; student maps each fact to a factor and writes a short conclusion
No scaffold; student identifies the relevant factors and applies them unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Which s 3 factors are most directly engaged in weighing this applicant's claim.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 3(1) requires the court to weigh, among other things, the applicant's financial resources and needs (now and in the foreseeable future), any disability of the applicant, the beneficiary's financial resources and needs, and the size and nature of the estate.
modelAnswer.application: The applicant's disability and limited earning capacity engage both the disability factor and the foreseeable-needs factor directly. The beneficiary's comparative financial comfort weakens any competing claim on the estate's limited resources, and the estate's modest size sharpens the practical trade-off the court must make between the two.
modelAnswer.conclusion: These four factors together point towards a reasonably strong claim, though the outcome still depends on the overall weighing exercise, including any factors not present on these facts.

parts.heading: Estrangement, animal charities, and the Ilott litigation
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story in full before extracting the doctrine
body: Heather Ilott left her mother's home at seventeen to live with a man her mother disapproved of; the two were estranged for the following two decades, with only a handful of failed attempted reconciliations. Heather's mother, Melita Jackson, made a will leaving her entire estate to three animal charities and explicitly nothing to Heather, together with a letter of wishes explaining why.

Heather, an independent adult with modest means, five children, and no expectation of inheritance, applied under the 1975 Act. The case went through multiple rounds of appeal over roughly a decade — the sums involved were modest relative to the litigation cost, which is itself a point examiners like to draw out. The Court of Appeal at one stage substantially increased Heather's award; the Supreme Court restored the original, more modest first-instance figure.

The Supreme Court's judgment is important less for the amount awarded than for what it declined to establish: it firmly rejected the idea that there is a settled 'legitimate expectation' test, or any freestanding principle that an adult child needs a 'moral claim' beyond the statutory maintenance standard, to succeed. The exercise remains the ordinary s 3 weighing exercise — estrangement and the testator's clearly expressed wishes are simply weighed as part of it, under the 'conduct' and 'obligations' limbs, rather than as a separate legal hurdle.

components.factsShort: An estranged adult daughter, excluded entirely from her mother's will in favour of animal charities, claimed maintenance under the 1975 Act.
components.ratioShort: There is no separate 'moral claim' test for an adult child; the ordinary s 3 weighing exercise applies, with estrangement and the testator's wishes going to weight rather than to a threshold requirement.

expanded.facts: Heather Ilott had been estranged from her mother for around 26 years by the time of her mother's death. Her mother's will left the entire estate, worth roughly £486,000, to three animal charities with which she had no connection during her life, and expressly excluded Heather. Heather and her husband lived on a modest income and state benefits, with five children.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that the district judge at first instance had been entitled to award Heather £50,000, being an amount assessed by reference to her maintenance needs, and restored that figure after the Court of Appeal had substantially increased it. The Court emphasised that the assessment is a fact-specific weighing exercise under s 3, not a search for a 'moral claim' or 'legitimate expectation' as a separate legal test.
expanded.significance: Ilott confirms that an adult child's claim is not barred by independence or estrangement, but nor is it assisted by any special doctrine — the s 3 factors, including the deceased's reasons and the length and cause of any estrangement, are simply weighed as they would be for any other applicant confined to the maintenance standard.

interaction.prompt: Did the Supreme Court in Ilott v Mitson hold that an adult child must show a distinct 'moral claim' on top of the ordinary s 3 factors to succeed?
options: No — it rejected any separate moral-claim or legitimate-expectation test
Yes — a moral claim is a freestanding legal requirement for adult children
Yes, but only where the child was estranged for more than ten years
No — the s 3 factors do not apply to adult children at all
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the Court was clear that the ordinary s 3 weighing exercise governs, with estrangement and the deceased's reasons feeding into it as factors, not as a separate hurdle to clear first.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what the Supreme Court actually rejected: a freestanding 'moral claim' or 'legitimate expectation' test. The s 3 factors still apply in the normal way, with estrangement simply weighed as part of that exercise.

parts.heading: Why an independent adult child still faces an uphill task
parts.voice: argumentative — explains the practical reality behind the formal legal position
body: If there is no separate legal test for adult children, why do they so often lose? The honest answer is that the maintenance standard itself, applied to someone who is not a minor and not incapacitated, tends to produce a high bar in practice — not because the law singles them out, but because of what 'maintenance' means and what the s 3 factors typically show for this kind of applicant.

An adult child with their own income, their own household, and no disability will often struggle to show that they currently need maintenance from the estate at all — the first hurdle in any maintenance-standard claim. Courts have also been cautious about awards that would effectively fund a change in lifestyle, rather than meet an actual, demonstrated need; Ilott's award, capped as it was, reflects exactly this caution.

What tends to move the needle for an adult child is evidence of a real, current need — poor health, insecure housing, low income relative to outgoings — combined with s 3 factors that cut the other way for any competing beneficiaries, such as those beneficiaries already being financially comfortable. Estrangement caused substantially by the deceased's own conduct, rather than the applicant's choices, can also carry weight under the 'conduct' limb, though it is rarely decisive alone.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that an adult child's claim automatically fails, or automatically requires proof of a 'moral obligation', because 'the law is harder on adult children'.
components.whyItsWrong: There is no such rule as a matter of law — Ilott explicitly rejects a separate moral-claim test. The practical difficulty adult children face comes from applying the ordinary maintenance standard and the ordinary s 3 factors to someone who typically has their own resources and no legal entitlement to be treated as dependent, not from any distinct heightened legal test.

interaction.prompt: Two adult children apply under the 1975 Act against the same estate. One has a stable income and owns her home outright; the other has a chronic illness limiting his ability to work and rents privately on a low income. Which is more likely to succeed on the merits, applying ordinary s 3 reasoning?
options: The child with the chronic illness and low income — his current and foreseeable needs are more clearly engaged
The child who owns her home outright — property ownership strengthens a maintenance claim
Neither — adult children can never succeed under the 1975 Act
Both equally — s 3 does not distinguish between applicants' financial circumstances
interaction.explanation: The maintenance standard and the s 3 factors turn heavily on demonstrated current and foreseeable need. The financially secure homeowner will struggle to show unmet maintenance needs, while the applicant with a chronic illness and low income has a materially stronger factual basis for a claim.

parts.heading: The six-month time limit
parts.voice: statute-first — puts the provision on the page before the practical consequences
body: A claim under the 1975 Act must, as a general rule, be brought within six months of the date on which representation (the grant of probate or letters of administration) is first taken out. This is a strict procedural rule sitting entirely separately from the merits-based s 3 analysis — a claim with overwhelming merits can still be shut out if it is brought too late, absent the court's permission.

Section 4 gives the court a discretion to allow a claim out of time, but it is not a formality — factors the court considers include how promptly the applicant acted once they knew the position, whether negotiations were ongoing, whether the estate has already been distributed (making an out-of-time claim more prejudicial to beneficiaries who have already received and potentially spent their inheritance), and the strength of the applicant's case on the merits.

Practitioners commonly protect a client's position, where the six months is running out and negotiations are unresolved, by entering a standstill agreement with the personal representatives rather than relying on the court's discretion to extend time — that discretion exists, but it is safer practice not to need it.

components.citation: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 4
components.text: An application for an order under section 2 of this Act shall not, except with the permission of the court, be made after the end of the period of six months from the date on which representation with respect to the estate of the deceased is first taken out.
elements: Application must be made within six months
Time runs from the date representation is first taken out
The court may permit a late application
No fixed formula for permission — a discretionary decision on the facts

interaction.prompt: From what date does the six-month time limit for a 1975 Act claim run?
options: The date representation is first taken out
The date of the deceased's death
The date the applicant first learns the terms of the will
The date the estate is fully distributed
interaction.explanation: Section 4 fixes the clock to the grant of representation, not the date of death or the date the applicant becomes aware of the will's contents — a distinction that can matter significantly if there is a delay in applying for the grant.

parts.heading: Putting the pieces together
parts.voice: direct — consolidates the lesson's moving parts against a single fact pattern
body: A complete 1975 Act analysis on the SQE1 moves through the same three stages every time: eligibility under s 1 (the previous lesson), the discretionary s 3 factors weighed against the applicable standard of provision, and the s 4 time limit. A strong answer checks all three — a common way to lose marks is jumping straight to the merits without first confirming eligibility and timing.

Contrast two applicants against the same estate to see the factors pull in different directions at once. A financially independent adult son, on good terms with his late father but expecting nothing, has a weak claim: no demonstrated need, no disability, no particular obligation owed to him specifically, and a will that reflects a deliberate, considered choice. A long-term cohabitant of the deceased, maintained by him for years and now facing housing insecurity, presents a materially stronger claim on the same core factors — need, obligation, and the size of the estate all point the same way.

The lesson's structural point is this: the 1975 Act does not ask whether a will was 'fair' in the abstract. It asks a narrower, factor-driven question — for this applicant, in this category, against this estate, was reasonable financial provision made — and it asks it within a strict procedural window.

components.definition: The court's overall, fact-specific evaluation of a 1975 Act claim, drawing on the applicant's and beneficiaries' resources and needs, the deceased's obligations, the size of the estate, disability, and conduct — none of which is individually decisive, and all of which are assessed against the standard of provision applicable to that applicant's category.

interaction.prompt: Applying the s 3 factors, which applicant has the stronger claim on the facts given?
interaction.scenarioA: An adult son, financially secure and in good health, who was on good terms with his late father and had no expectation of inheriting under the will, which left everything to charity.
interaction.scenarioB: A long-term cohabitant of the deceased, financially maintained by him for over a decade, who now faces losing her home because the will left the entire estate to a distant relative she has never met.
interaction.explanation: Scenario B engages need, the deceased's established obligation towards her through years of maintenance, and the size of the estate relative to that need, all pointing the same way. Scenario A shows no demonstrated need, no disability, and no particular obligation — a materially weaker claim even though he is eligible to apply at all.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is a core factor the court must consider under s 3(1) of the 1975 Act?
options: The size and nature of the estate
The applicant's religious beliefs
Whether the deceased left a letter of wishes explaining the will
The applicant's political views
testPool.explanation: The size and nature of the estate is expressly listed in s 3(1) — it shapes what is practically achievable, regardless of how strong an applicant's need otherwise is.

testPool.prompt: Under s 4 of the 1975 Act, what is the standard time limit for bringing a claim?
options: Six months from the date representation is first taken out
Twelve months from the date of death
Three months from the date the will is read
There is no time limit for eligible applicants
testPool.explanation: Section 4 sets a six-month limit running from the grant of representation, subject to the court's discretion to permit a late claim.

testPool.prompt: According to Ilott v Mitson, what did the Supreme Court say about the legal test applicable to an adult child's claim?
options: There is no separate 'moral claim' test; the ordinary s 3 factors apply
An adult child must always show a moral claim distinct from need
Adult children are excluded from claiming unless disabled
The maintenance standard does not apply to adult children
testPool.explanation: The Court rejected any freestanding moral-claim or legitimate-expectation requirement, applying the ordinary s 3 weighing exercise instead.

testPool.prompt: A trainee is asked why an independent adult child's claim is often harder to establish in practice than, say, a maintained cohabitant's claim. What is the best explanation?
options: The maintenance standard and s 3 factors typically show less demonstrated need where the applicant is financially independent
The 1975 Act formally excludes adult children unless they are disabled
A separate, higher legal test applies specifically to adult children
Adult children cannot rely on the 'conduct' factor under s 3
testPool.explanation: The difficulty is practical rather than doctrinal — it flows from applying the ordinary maintenance standard and s 3 factors to someone who typically has fewer demonstrated needs, not from any distinct legal bar.

testPool.prompt: A trainee argues that because the Court of Appeal significantly increased Heather Ilott's award before the Supreme Court reduced it again, the case shows that adult children generally receive large awards. Is this a fair reading of the case?
options: No — the Supreme Court restored the more modest first-instance figure, and the case is notable for rejecting a special test, not for the size of the award
Yes — the final, binding figure was the larger Court of Appeal award
Yes — the case establishes a benchmark award for all adult child claims
No — the Supreme Court held adult children should never receive substantial awards
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to focus on the highest figure reached during the litigation, but the Supreme Court's decision — the binding outcome — restored the original, more modest award. The case's real significance lies in its rejection of a separate legal test, not in setting a benchmark sum.

testPool.prompt: An applicant's claim under the 1975 Act is filed eight months after the grant of probate, with no application for the court's permission to bring it late. What is the correct position?
options: The claim is out of time and requires the court's permission to proceed, which is not automatic
The claim is automatically valid, since six months is only a guideline
The claim is barred permanently with no possibility of proceeding
The time limit only applies to spouse applicants, so this claim can proceed regardless
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to treat six months as either an absolute bar or a loose guideline, but it is neither — the claim is out of time on its face, but s 4 gives the court a genuine discretion to permit it to proceed if the applicant seeks and obtains that permission.

testPool.prompt: A beneficiary argues that because the deceased's will included a detailed letter of wishes explaining why an adult daughter was excluded, the daughter's 1975 Act claim must automatically fail. Is this correct?
options: No — the deceased's reasons are relevant as part of the s 3 weighing exercise but are not automatically decisive
Yes — a documented letter of wishes is a complete defence to any claim
No — letters of wishes are never admissible in 1975 Act proceedings
Yes, but only if the letter was signed by a solicitor as witness
testPool.trapExplanation: A clearly reasoned letter of wishes feels like it should settle the matter, and it is genuinely relevant conduct evidence — but Ilott confirms the court still carries out the full s 3 weighing exercise; the deceased's reasons are weighed, not treated as an automatic bar.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is closest to a correct description of what s 3(1) requires the court to consider?
options: A non-exhaustive list of factors including resources and needs of applicants and beneficiaries, obligations, estate size, disability, and conduct
A fixed, exhaustive checklist where every factor must point the same way for a claim to succeed
Only the financial resources of the applicant, to the exclusion of the beneficiaries' circumstances
A single overriding test of whether the will was 'fair' in the eyes of a reasonable person
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to picture s 3 as either a rigid checklist or a vague fairness test, but it is neither — it is a non-exhaustive list of specific factors that the court weighs together, none of which alone decides the outcome.

testPool.prompt: An applicant with a serious, long-term illness that prevents full-time work applies against an estate where the sole beneficiary is financially comfortable and the estate itself is substantial. Which combination of s 3 factors most strongly supports the applicant's claim?
options: The applicant's disability and foreseeable needs, the beneficiary's comfortable resources, and the size of the estate
The applicant's political opinions and the beneficiary's personal habits
The length of time since the deceased's death and the applicant's religious views
The applicant's age alone, considered in isolation from every other factor
testPool.explanation: Disability and foreseeable need, weighed against a comparatively resourced beneficiary and a substantial estate capable of accommodating an award, are exactly the combination s 3 is built to capture.

testPool.prompt: Representation in an estate was first taken out on 1 March. An eligible applicant wants to bring a 1975 Act claim but has not yet issued proceedings by 15 September of the same year. What is the correct advice?
options: The claim is out of time, having missed the six-month deadline of 1 September, so permission to proceed late will need to be sought
The claim is still in time, since the six months runs from the date of death, not the grant
The claim can never proceed now under any circumstances
The deadline is calculated from 15 September itself, so there is no issue
testPool.explanation: Six months from 1 March expires on 1 September. By 15 September the ordinary window has closed, and the applicant needs the court's permission under s 4 to bring the claim out of time.

testPool.prompt: A financially secure adult daughter, who was never maintained by her father and has no disability, brings a 1975 Act claim purely on the basis that she feels the will's distribution was emotionally unfair. Applying s 3 as interpreted in Ilott, how is this claim likely to be assessed?
options: Weakly — without demonstrated need, disability, or a relevant obligation, a bare sense of unfairness does not by itself satisfy the maintenance standard
Strongly — any adult child who feels excluded automatically succeeds under s 3
It cannot be assessed at all, since adult children are ineligible to apply
Strongly — emotional unfairness is itself listed as a s 3(1) factor
testPool.explanation: Ilott confirms there is no free-standing fairness or moral-claim test. Without evidence going to the actual s 3 factors — need, disability, obligation — a claim resting only on a sense of unfairness is unlikely to meet the maintenance standard.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best reflects the effect of s 3(1)(g) of the 1975 Act (the 'any other matter, including conduct' limb)?
options: It gives the court an open-ended power to weigh relevant matters, such as estrangement, that do not fit neatly into the other listed factors
It restricts the court to considering only the factors expressly listed elsewhere in s 3(1)
It applies only to claims by a spouse or civil partner
It automatically disqualifies an applicant whose conduct towards the deceased was poor
testPool.explanation: This limb is deliberately broad, allowing the court to bring in matters like estrangement or the deceased's own conduct as part of the overall weighing exercise, without any automatic disqualifying effect.

testPool.prompt: Which Act and section together set the six-month time limit for bringing a family provision claim?
options: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 4
Administration of Estates Act 1925, s 46
Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975, s 1
Limitation Act 1980, s 2
testPool.explanation: Section 4 of the 1975 Act — not the general Limitation Act, and not s 1 (which deals with eligibility, not timing) — fixes the six-month period.

testPool.prompt: The court's discretion under s 4 to permit a late claim is best described as which of the following?
options: A genuine discretion exercised on the facts, having regard to matters such as promptness, ongoing negotiations, and prejudice to beneficiaries
An automatic extension available on request without any further evidence
Unavailable in practice, regardless of the circumstances
Limited to spouse applicants only
testPool.explanation: Section 4 gives a real, fact-sensitive discretion — not a rubber stamp and not an absolute bar — which practitioners generally try not to have to rely on given its uncertainty.

testPool.prompt: An applicant with strong maintenance needs delays bringing a claim for ten months after the grant of representation, during which time she was engaged in without-prejudice settlement negotiations with the personal representatives that ultimately broke down. What is the most accurate assessment of her position?
options: She is out of time under s 4 and will need the court's permission, though the ongoing negotiations may support that application
She is automatically barred, since negotiations do not affect the strict six-month limit
She is still in time, since negotiations pause the running of the time limit automatically
She is in time because the limit runs from the end of any negotiations, not the grant of representation
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to assume ongoing negotiations either stop the clock automatically or are irrelevant — neither is right. The six-month period still runs from the grant, so she is technically out of time, but the history of genuine negotiations is exactly the kind of fact the court can take into account in deciding whether to permit a late claim.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring trap is treating either the deceased's stated reasons or an applicant's estrangement as automatically decisive one way or the other. Ilott's real lesson is that both are simply weighed within the ordinary s 3 exercise — and a second, quieter trap is forgetting to check the six-month clock before getting absorbed in the merits.
